blocks.body: Fixtures below the sewer line, like a basement bathroom or laundry, drain into a sealed basin. The ejector pump lifts that wastewater up into the main line. A float turns it on and a check valve keeps water from falling back. When any part fails, those fixtures back up.

blocks.h2: How to Protect Your Ejector Pump
blocks.body: Only toilet paper and waste should go down a toilet that drains to an ejector pump. Wipes, paper towels and feminine products wrap around the impeller and stall it. Grease from a basement kitchen or bar sink hardens in the basin. Test the alarm once in a while by lifting the float, if you can do it safely. And have the basin checked when you notice odors, slow drains or a pump that runs more than it should.

blocks.h2: Ejector Pump Questions From Evanston Homeowners

items.q: My ejector pump alarm is going off. What should I do?
items.preview: Stop using basement fixtures and call us.
items.answer: Stop using every fixture that drains to the basin and call us.

items.q: What's the difference between a sump pump and an ejector pump?
items.answer: A [sump pump](/evanston/sump-pumps) moves groundwater. An ejector pump moves wastewater from basement fixtures.

items.q: How long do ejector pumps last?
Why does it smell like sewer near the pit?
items.preview: A seal, vent or dry trap.
items.answer: Usually a worn lid seal, a vent problem or a dry floor drain trap.

items.q: Can you replace just the pump?
items.answer: Usually. If the basin and piping are in good shape, we replace only the pump.

items.q: How much does ejector pump replacement cost in Evanston?
items.preview: It depends on the pump and basin. You'll approve a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on the pump, the basin and access. You'll approve a flat-rate price before we start.
